transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 58m
Attendees: Ari Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Head of ML, Pinecrest), Ethan Ruiz (CTO), Sana Ahmed (Cloud Infra), Liam O'Neil (Product)

Summary: Short discovery focused on Dedicated capacity — reserved GPUs, isolation (data and network), burst-to-hosted behavior, and scaling expectations. Customer wants cost predictability and compliance controls; primary use cases are real-time chat assistant and nightly batch embeddings for search.

[00:00] Ari: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Ari, AE on Redwood. Jordan's our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:08] Maya: Good thanks, Maya here. Sorry for the slight echo on my side, we have a few people on different mics.
[00:12] Ethan: Ethan here. We kicked off because we want to evaluate dedicated GPU pools for some of our in-house assistants, correct.
[00:18] Ari: Exactly. High level agenda: understand your workloads, latency and throughput targets, security and compliance needs, and then map to Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private. We'll also talk about burst policy and scaling.
[00:28] Jordan: Quick note — when we say Dedicated we mean reserved GPU pools with customer isolation, optional private networking and encryption by default. You can pin model versions and set autoscale rules.
[00:36] Sana: Curious — we already run some RAG and a vector search pipeline on GCP, and we use SageMaker endpoints for a few models. We want more predictable unit economics and SLOs.
[00:45] Ari: Makes sense. Could you walk us through traffic patterns? QPS, peak windows, and tail latency requirements?
[00:52] Maya: Sure. Typical day: 15 qps avg for chat, spikes up to 120 qps during business hours for short prompts, many requests short context <512 tokens. Nightly batch embedding jobs — about 3M records weekly, spread across a 6 hour window. Latency target for chat is 150-250ms p50 and under 600ms p95 — we know that's aggressive.
[01:18] Jordan: Okay that helps. For Dedicated we size pools by GPU and concurrent slots. For example, an A100-style instance with optimized batching can handle X concurrent sessions for 512 tokens average; we'll run benchmarks. Do you expect steady concurrency or very bursty?
[01:32] Maya: It's bursty — big spikes when promo emails go out and call center use. We also want the ability to burst to hosted during big spikes but keep isolation for sensitive flows.
[01:44] Ethan: Important — we cannot send certain PII or payment flows outside our VPC. So some traffic must stay on Dedicated or Private. Others can burst to Hosted for elasticity if masked.
[01:57] Jordan: That lines up with our hybrid routing policy. We support tag-based routing: route traffic by policy (sensitivity, latency tier). You can set fallbacks to Hosted or lower-tier models automatically when capacity constrained. Note, the fallback will depend on whether your data is allowed to leave the Dedicated environment.
[02:12] Sana: How does the network isolation actually work? We have strict VPC peering requirements and need to understand egress controls and NAT behavior.
[02:19] Jordan: Dedicated can be deployed into a private VPC peering arrangement or via Private deployment options — we can do customer-managed VPC and private link. We also provide audit logs and per-request cryptographic signatures. There was a doc on VPC peering, I'll share the link.
[02:34] Maya: Great. On security — SOC 2, encryption at rest, KMS. Do you have HSM/KMS integrations? We need to ensure keys are customer-controlled.
[02:42] Ari: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations in Private and Dedicated, with full audit logs. We'll share SOC2 report and our security pack after the call.
[02:51] Ethan: What about patching and maintenance windows? We need guaranteed uptime and predictable maintenance.
[02:57] Jordan: For Dedicated we provide SLA-backed uptime tiers. Maintenance windows are scheduled and communicated; we offer replica pools and can route traffic to standby nodes during maintenance for critical routes.
[03:08] Maya: Pricing question — is Dedicated purely committed monthly, or is there some hybrid where we commit baseline and then pay for bursts?
[03:15] Ari: We offer reserved capacity with commit tiers plus burst credits. Typical model: commit to N GPU-equivalent units monthly for a discount, and have burst capacity at defined rates. Burst pricing is higher but gives elasticity. You can also set hard caps so no surprise charges.
[03:28] Ethan: Can you define how bursting works technically? Is it pre-warmed or `cold` spin-up? We care about the tail latency when bursting.
[03:36] Jordan: Option matrix: 1) pre-warmed burst nodes — keep a small pool warm to handle predictable bursts (best latency, higher cost); 2) cold spin-up — can add nodes from spare capacity or Hosted, which takes a minute(s) and impacts p95; 3) model fallback — route to smaller, cheaper model variants for graceful degradation. For most customers we do a combination: pre-warm for frequent predictable spikes and fallback to hosted or lighter models for very large irregular spikes.
[04:03] Sana: For our compliance flows we need zero-data-exfil for certain endpoints. That means those routes cannot ever hit Hosted. Can we set per-route policies?
[04:11] Jordan: Yes, route-level policies with tags. You can mark endpoints as "no-extern" and Redwood will never offload them. Those endpoints would have to be served within your Dedicated / Private environment.
[04:20] Liam: What's the typical lead time to provision a Dedicated pool and to scale it up? We are planning a pilot in six weeks.
[04:26] Ari: Provisioning a basic Dedicated pool can be as fast as 1-2 weeks depending on region and capacity; for VPC/private deployments possibly 3-4 weeks if there's network approvals. Scaling up within an existing pool is faster — autoscale rules apply, and adding GPU capacity can be done in hours to days.
[04:41] Maya: Benchmarks — we want to run our prompts and see token cost and latency. Do you do P0 benchmarks for customers?
[04:47] Jordan: Yes, we run a 24-72 hour benchmark with your sample workload. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and cache/kv hit rates. We'll share a spreadsheet and a dashboard.
[04:58] Ethan: For embeddings — do you recommend running embeddings on the same pool or separate batch workers? We have heavy nightly batches.
[05:04] Jordan: We usually separate batch embedding workers from low-latency chat pools to avoid noisy neighbors inside your own pool; dedicated clusters for batch jobs scheduled off-peak is common. We also support job queues and spot-like capacity for large batches.
[05:16] Sana: How does key rotation and audit log retention work? We need 1 year of detailed RPC logs for investigations.
[05:22] Ari: We can configure audit retention tiers; by default we keep logs for 90 days, extended retention is available as an add-on. Key rotation can be customer-driven using KMS; we integrate with common KMS providers.
[05:34] Maya: Any notable gotchas on model quantization or performance degradation when you quantize? We're running some Llama and Claude style open models.
[05:41] Jordan: Quantization will save cost but can slightly change output quality; our runtime supports quantization-aware execution and we recommend running evals on your prompt set. We'll provide suggested quantization profiles per model and workload.
[05:52] Liam: Stakeholders — who's the exec sponsor on our side?
[05:55] Maya: CTO (Ethan) is sponsoring, and product owns rollout. Security and infra will be gating.
[05:59] Ari: Good — we'll coordinate security review with Sana.
[06:02] Jordan: Quick note on observability: Redwood Console gives per-route token cost, latency dashboards, traces and an evals module for regression alerts.
[06:10] Ethan: For billing — will we get monthly breakdown by route, model and token type?
[06:15] Ari: Yes we expose token-level cost breakdowns and can map costs to routes, tags, and teams.
[06:19] Maya: Any references or docs you can share now?
[06:22] Ari: I'll drop links to the Dedicated datasheet, the VPC peering guide, SOC2 pack and the benchmarking spreadsheet after the call.
[06:29] Sana: Ok, let's talk about the pilot. We'll do a pilot with one chat flow (sensitive) on Dedicated, and non-sensitive flows on Hosted for burst. We'll provide sample workload and expect a benchmark run.
[06:40] Jordan: Sounds good. For pilot sizing — can you provide expected avg tokens per request and concurrency for that flow?
[06:45] Maya: Avg tokens ~220, typical concurrency 8, peak 40 for that flow.
[06:51] Jordan: Great, we'll draft a capacity plan and suggested GPU mix (e.g., 4x A100 equiv for baseline with 2x warm burst nodes) and include cost estimates.
[07:02] Discussion continues with clarifying network ACLs, egress policies and SSO integration.
[07:30] Ethan: One more question — how do upgrades and model rollouts work? Can we do canary and automatic fallback?
[07:36] Jordan: Yes, Canary and A/B rollouts are supported. You can route a percentage of traffic, and automatic fallback policies if latency or error thresholds breach.
[07:45] Maya: Any legal/procurement steps we should expect?
[07:48] Ari: We'll share a standard SOW and MSLA. Procurement typically reviews SOC2, encryption docs and a data processing addendum. We'll work with your legal team.
[07:58] Closing recap:
- Redwood to send Dedicated pricing, SOW, SOC2/security pack, VPC guide, and link to benchmark template.
- Pinecrest to provide 24-hour sample workload, top prompts and latency targets.
- Jordan to prepare preliminary capacity plan and burst options.

[08:20] Ari: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and schedule the security deep-dive.
[08:24] Maya: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:26] Ethan: Thanks all.

Notes: Transcript contains a few small transcription errors (e.g., "KV cash" instead of KV cache in one auto-note) and some speaker overlaps.
